Problem 371. Pairwise collective choice: Park versus Library
Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.

Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 4 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 5 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 2 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.
For a pairwise contest, count how many voters prefer each of the two options. Ignore the third option for that comparison.
In a pairwise vote between Park and Library, which option wins?
1. For each group, check whether Park or Library is ranked higher. 2. Totals: Park=6, Library=5. 3. Therefore the result is Park.
A collective decision rule must be explicit; different rules can summarize the same rankings differently.
Preference rankings; for pair (a,b), sum weights of voters ranking a>b versus b>a.

Part B — New and mixed reasoning domains
Map scale links a model to the real world through proportional reasoning.
A map has scale 1:10000. The measured map distance between two points is 4 cm. Rule: 1 cm on the map represents 10000 cm in reality; 100,000 cm = 1 km.
Multiply map length by the scale denominator, then convert units. A scale is a ratio, not an added distance.
What is the real straight-line distance in kilometres?
Scale problems are ratio problems: keep units explicit and conversion becomes mechanical.
Proportion d_real=d_map×denominator, followed by unit conversion.

Problem 381. Locating a point by constraints: case 1
Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.
A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 6. It satisfies x+y=4 and x−y=0.
A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.
Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?
1. List pairs satisfying x+y=4. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=0. 3. The remaining set is [(2, 2)].
A constraint problem is solved by satisfying all conditions together, not one at a time independently.
Problem 382. Locating a point by constraints: case 2
Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.
A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 6. It satisfies x+y=7 and x−y=-1.
A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.
Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?
1. List pairs satisfying x+y=7. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=-1. 3. The remaining set is [(3, 4)].
